title: A Repair Is Not an Order
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 41 · The Seventh Ring arc
content:
The first warning came in the shape of a wrench.

I had lent it to Brasswatch Yard three weeks earlier. It was an ugly thing with a chipped red handle, too valuable to lose and too ordinary to deserve a story. Danse had promised to mark it with our initials before returning it.

Instead it came back in a crate addressed to Ba Sing Se.

Danse stared at the label.

“That's not where the workshop is.”

“Brilliant deduction.”

He lifted the wrench from its wrapping. The mark was still on the handle. Everything about it was ours except the destination.

I watched the old tension gather between his shoulders.

“You're making the officer face,” I said.

“The what?”

“The one that says all the nouns in the room have been promoted to problems.”

He gave me a look. Then he set the wrench down and reached for the paper.

The note from Neri explained that goods were arriving through the wrong doors. There had been no injuries. A medical delivery had been delayed. Someone had bent one of the brass teeth beneath the Lanternwell and tried to hide the repair.

Danse read that sentence twice.

“That's sabotage.”

“Maybe. It might also be a bad repair.”

“An unauthorized modification.”

“That too.”

He looked offended that I would distinguish between the two.

We traveled to Brasswatch Yard after breakfast. On our side of the threshold, the Commonwealth smelled of hot dust and rust. On the other, the yard held clean air, damp wood, and the metallic tang of people who tried to fix everything with tools that didn't quite fit.

Danse knew most of them by name.

He stopped beside the youngest apprentice, a girl called Len, who was using a file to shape a narrow strip of brass. The metal sat too close to the edge of the workbench. He noticed before she did.

“Secure your workpiece,” he said.

Len looked up. Her eyes flicked to his hands.

“Please,” he added.

It was such a small word. I wanted to take his hand for having remembered it.

Instead I handed him the box of returned tools and told him to sort them. He made a noise of disapproval and did exactly that.

Neri arrived with Toph, who immediately asked why the yard had so many chairs and so few functioning stools. Toph and Danse recognized one another's expertise in roughly the same way two storm fronts recognize the same valley.

“Show me the gear,” Toph said.

“First I need the full assembly diagram.”

“You can look at a diagram all day and still miss what the metal's doing.”

“And you can infer the damage without understanding its load requirements.”

Toph grinned. “Well. This is going to be fun.”

I took Neri aside before the demonstration became a professional duel.

“What do you know about the labels?”

“Someone copied the old keeper marks onto newer tags.”

“Who?”

“We have no record of it. That's part of the problem.”

I turned one of the new tags over. The ink had bled into the fibers. The handwriting was neat. The string was knotted twice, using a method I recognized from the Commonwealth. Not a magical trick. A practical knot tied by somebody who wanted a parcel to stay attached.

“There are six different destination names,” I said. “But the same hand wrote them all.”

Neri nodded.

“One person doesn't have to be dangerous to make a dangerous system,” Danse said behind us.

He had followed silently enough to make me jump.

“You can't keep doing that.”

“I wasn't trying to startle you.”

“That's somehow worse.”

He looked at the tags. His expression had changed, no longer eager to identify a culprit. More thoughtful.

“When I was in the Brotherhood, a uniform could become an answer to a question nobody had asked. If a superior officer signed a form, people assumed the reasoning had already happened.”

I waited.

His eyes met mine.

“I thought that was discipline.”

“What do you call it now?”

“Sometimes necessary. Sometimes cowardice.”

He said it without performing regret. He'd spent too long learning the cost of the distinction to make it beautiful.

Toph arrived holding the damaged brass tooth.

“Somebody bent this to make the wheels turn faster,” she said. “And shaved the sides so it wouldn't catch. That's why it failed.”

Danse examined it.

“Whoever did it understood the machine.”

“Enough to make it worse,” Toph said.

“That's still understanding.”

I could have kissed them both for arriving at an argument useful enough to share.

Instead I asked Len whether she knew the tool marks.

She looked at the brass, then away. The silence held long enough to become an answer.

“I saw the new keeper working on it,” she said.

Neri's face went white. “What new keeper?”

Len pointed toward the old records room.

A person named Orren had been organizing deliveries for weeks. They had a borrowed apron, a careful way of speaking, and no appointment from any of the six districts. People had allowed them to help because the shelves looked better afterward.

The room was empty when we entered. Inside lay a ledger with one page torn out.

Danse touched the torn edge.

“We find the missing records,” he said.

Neri started toward the door.

“Not like that,” I told her.

She looked startled.

“We tell the districts what happened first. We don't send strangers after someone because we're embarrassed we let them handle our mail.”

Danse turned to me. He hesitated, then nodded.

“Acknowledged.”

I leaned against the desk. “That might be the most romantic word you've ever said.”

He raised one eyebrow. “I've said others.”

“Oh, have you?”

His hand found mine in the shadow beside the filing cabinet. He did not pull me closer until I stepped toward him. His kiss was brief, warm, and unexpectedly amused.

When we came apart, Toph was standing in the doorway.

“Gross,” she said.

“Do you ever knock?” I asked.

“On an open door? No.”

Danse looked as though he wanted to court-martial the entire afternoon.

Toph lifted the brass tooth. “Are we fixing this or what?”

“We're making a safe temporary replacement,” he said. “Then we're asking the people who use the doors what they need the permanent system to do.”

She smiled.

It took me a moment to realize that was her version of approval.

By evening the wrench was back in our workshop. The damaged gear remained under examination. The list of missing parcels was longer than before, but this time every item had a real person to call.

Danse added a note to our ledger.

NO ORDERS ACCEPTED WITHOUT A REASON.

I looked at it for a long time.

Then I took the chipped red wrench and placed it back on its hook.

We had done one thing right. We had not mistaken the finding of a culprit for the repairing of a community.

Outside, the rain began to fall.

Inside, there was still work to do.
